title: WASSCE Further Maths: Calculus (Differentiation & Integration) - Further Mathematics - Turning Points
subject: Further Mathematics

questions.q: Find the x-coordinates of the turning points of $y = \frac{1}{3}x^3 - x^2 - 3x + 4$ and determine their nature.
options: $x=3$ is a maximum, $x=-1$ is a minimum
$x=3$ is a minimum, $x=-1$ is a maximum
questions.explain: Find turning points where $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$. $\frac{dy}{dx} = x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x-3)(x+1) = 0$, so $x=3$ and $x=-1$. The second derivative is $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2x - 2$. At $x=3$, $2(3)-2 = 4 > 0$ (Minimum). At $x=-1$, $2(-1)-2 = -4 < 0$ (Maximum).

questions.q: Find the x-coordinate of the turning point of the curve $y = x^2 - 6x + 5$.
questions.explain: A turning point occurs where the gradient is zero. Differentiate to get $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x - 6$. Set it to zero: $2x - 6 = 0$, leading to $x = 3$.

questions.q: Find the coordinates of the turning point of the curve $y = -x^2 + 4x + 1$.
questions.explain: Set the first derivative to zero: $\frac{dy}{dx} = -2x + 4 = 0$, which solves to $x = 2$. To find the y-coordinate, substitute $x = 2$ into the original equation: $y = -(2)^2 + 4(2) + 1 = -4 + 8 + 1 = 5$. Thus, the turning point is $(2, 5)$.

questions.q: Find the x-coordinates of all turning points of the curve $y = \frac{x^2}{x+2}$.
questions.explain: Using the quotient rule: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2x(x+2) - x^2(1)}{(x+2)^2} = \frac{2x^2 + 4x - x^2}{(x+2)^2} = \frac{x^2 + 4x}{(x+2)^2}$. Turning points occur where $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $x^2 + 4x = 0$, which factors as $x(x+4) = 0$. The roots are $x=0$ and $x=-4$.
